regions.name: Emilia-Romagna
regions.summary: Emilia-Romagna crosses northern Italy from Piacenza to the Adriatic at Rimini, with the Po to its north and the Apennines to its south, and it is two wine regions in one. Emilia, the western half around Modena and Reggio, is the home of Lambrusco, a family of red grapes made into frizzante wine, mostly in tank, and sold dry, medium sweet or sweet. Romagna, the eastern half from Imola to the sea, grows Sangiovese and Albana, which in 1987 became the first white wine in Italy raised to DOCG. The food of the region, Parmigiano Reggiano, prosciutto, mortadella and balsamic vinegar, explains its wines: fresh, fizzy and made for the table.

terroir.climate: The Court files the region as cool continental, and the Po plain fits it: cold, foggy winters, hot and humid summers and rain in spring and autumn. The Apennine foothills are a little cooler and better aired than the plain, and Romagna, open to the Adriatic, is milder and sunnier, with sea breezes reaching its hills. Fog and humidity bring rot and mildew; hail and spring frost are the other hazards.
terroir.soils: The plain is deep alluvium laid down by the Po and its Apennine tributaries: fertile silt, clay and sand. Sorbara's vineyards lie on lighter, sandier alluvium between the Secchia and the Panaro, while Grasparossa grows on the clay and marl of the foothills south of Modena. Romagna's hills are clay, marl and sandstone, crossed by a band of yellow, fossil-rich calcarenite the growers call spungone and by a ridge of gypsum near Brisighella.
terroir.topography: A long, flat plain falls gently from the mountains to the Po, cut by the Roman road, the Via Emilia, that strings the cities together: Piacenza, Parma, Reggio, Modena, Bologna, and in Romagna Imola, Faenza, Forlì, Cesena and Rimini. South of the road a band of low hills, the colli, rises towards the Apennine ridge, and that is where the finer vineyards sit: the Colli Piacentini, the Colli di Parma, the Colli Bolognesi and the Romagna hills.
terroir.water: The Po forms most of the northern border, and its tributaries, the Trebbia, Taro, Secchia, Panaro and Reno among them, run north out of the mountains across the plain. Their silt makes the plain fertile and their valleys draw cool air down from the hills. The Adriatic tempers eastern Romagna, and the sandy ground of the Po delta near Ferrara grows the Fortana of Bosco Eliceo.

grapes.name: Lambrusco di Sorbara
grapes.styles: The pale member of the family: it sets fruit poorly and gives thin bunches, so its wine is light ruby to deep pink, sharply acidic and scented with violets and sour cherry.

grapes.name: Lambrusco Grasparossa
grapes.styles: Named for its stalks, which turn red at harvest; grown in the foothills around Castelvetro, it gives dark, full and tannic Lambrusco, the opposite pole to Sorbara.

grapes.name: Lambrusco Salamino
grapes.styles: Named for its small, cylindrical bunches shaped like a salami; planted widely on the plain around Carpi and Reggio, it gives deep colour and round, fruity wine.

grapes.name: Ancellotta
grapes.styles: A deeply coloured red blended into Lambrusco, above all in Reggio Emilia, for colour and softness.

grapes.name: Sangiovese
grapes.styles: Romagna's red, grown on the hills from Imola to Rimini: sour cherry, violet and firm acid, light in plain Romagna Sangiovese and more structured in the Superiore, the Riserva and the subzone wines.

grapes.name: Albana
grapes.styles: Romagna's native white, thick skinned, with high acid and a little tannin for a white: dry wines with a bitter almond finish, and sweet passito from dried or botrytised grapes.

grapes.name: Trebbiano Romagnolo
grapes.styles: The workhorse white of the Romagna plain, neutral and productive, sold as Romagna Trebbiano and in IGT blends.

grapes.name: Pignoletto
grapes.styles: Grechetto Gentile by its variety name, grown in the Bologna hills for crisp still and frizzante whites with apple, herbs and a light bitter finish.

grapes.name: Malvasia di Candia Aromatica
grapes.styles: The aromatic white of the Piacenza and Parma hills, made dry, frizzante or passito, scented with orange blossom and peach.

grapes.name: Barbera
grapes.styles: With Croatina the base of Gutturnio, the red of the Piacenza hills, where it brings acid and bright fruit.

grapes.name: Croatina
grapes.styles: Called Bonarda in the Piacenza hills, it gives Gutturnio its colour, dark fruit and tannin.

wines.note: Pale ruby to deep pink, frothy and dry in its classic form, with violets, wild strawberry and sharp acidity. Serve it cold beside prosciutto, mortadella and gnocco fritto.
Deep purple with a violet foam, blackberry and plum and a dry, firm grip of tannin; the Lambrusco for zampone, cotechino and the rich pork dishes of Modena.
Deep ruby, fruity and round, dry or off dry; an all round partner for salumi and Parmigiano Reggiano.
Soft, grapey and medium sweet, often coloured with Ancellotta: the style of Reggio's large cooperatives that carried Lambrusco to American tables from the 1970s. Serve it well chilled.
Medium bodied, with sour cherry, violet and an earthy, savoury edge; the Superiore and Riserva wines of the hills carry more weight. Pour it with ragù, roast meats and piadina with cured ham.
Golden, full and faintly tannic, with apricot, almond and a bitter twist; serve it with fish stews, white meats and fresh cheeses.
From dried, often botrytised grapes: honey, apricot and saffron over fresh acidity, with blue cheese or almond pastries.
Barbera and Croatina from the Piacenza hills, still or frizzante: dark cherry, fresh acid and soft tannin, with coppa and the other salumi of Piacenza.

made.viticulture: On the plain, vines were long trained up trees in the old mixed farms, and today high, vigorous trellises such as the Sylvoz and the double curtain carry generous crops of Lambrusco and Trebbiano for the frizzante and bulk trade. The hill vineyards are trained lower, on spurred cordon or Guyot, and give smaller, riper crops. Lambrusco di Sorbara sets fruit poorly, which is why its DOC lets Salamino make up to 40 per cent of the wine. Albana's thick skins resist rot, so it can hang into the foggy autumn for passito or for noble rot. The hazards are fungal disease on the humid plain, spring frost in the hollows, summer hail and, more often now, drought in hot summers.
made.winemaking: Most Lambrusco is made in two steps: a dry base wine, then a second fermentation in a pressure tank, the Charmat or Martinotti method, stopped by chilling and filtering when the sparkle and the sweetness are right. Frizzante wines carry a light sparkle of about 1 to 2.5 bar, spumante a full one. The older way, refermentation in the bottle, leaves a cloudy sediment and has come back with small growers, and a few make Lambrusco by the traditional method or the ancestral method. Skin contact is short, so even dark Lambrusco is light in tannin, and Sorbara can be pressed almost as a rosé. Romagna's Sangiovese is fermented in steel or wood and aged in cask for Riserva; Albana passito comes from bunches dried on racks or picked late with noble rot; and the Piacenza hills keep a habit of skin fermented whites from Malvasia di Candia.

law.classification: Italian law sets the ladder: DOCG, DOC and IGT, the Italian name for an IGP. In 2026 Emilia-Romagna holds two DOCGs: Romagna Albana, raised in 1987 as Albana di Romagna, the first white DOCG in Italy, and Colli Bolognesi Pignoletto in the Bologna hills, raised in 2010. There is no single Lambrusco DOC. The Court lists Sorbara, Grasparossa di Castelvetro and Salamino di Santa Croce as subzones, but each is a DOC of its own, all three recognised in 1970, beside the broader Reggiano and Modena DOCs. A great deal of Lambrusco is sold as IGT Emilia, also written dell'Emilia. The Romagna DOC covers Sangiovese, Trebbiano and sparkling wines and lets a Sangiovese name one of its subzones. In the west, the Colli Piacentini DOC and the Gutturnio DOC, separated from it in 2010, hold the Piacenza hills.
tiers: Romagna Albana DOCG
Albana from the Romagna hills, secco, amabile, dolce or passito; raised in 1987 as Albana di Romagna, the first white DOCG in Italy.
Colli Bolognesi Pignoletto DOCG
Whites of Grechetto Gentile from the hills south-west of Bologna, DOCG since 2010; its Classico wine takes at least 95 per cent Grechetto Gentile.
Lambrusco di Sorbara DOC
At least 60 per cent Sorbara, the rest mainly Salamino; frizzante or spumante, secco to dolce.
Lambrusco Grasparossa di Castelvetro DOC
At least 85 per cent Grasparossa, from the plain and foothills south of Modena.
Lambrusco Salamino di Santa Croce DOC
Salamino led, from the plain around Carpi, north of Modena.
Reggiano DOC and Modena DOC
The broader Lambrusco DOCs of the two provinces, blends of several Lambrusco varieties, often softened with Ancellotta in Reggio.
Romagna DOC
Sangiovese, Trebbiano and sparkling wines across Romagna; Romagna Sangiovese may add Superiore, Riserva and a subzone name.
Gutturnio DOC
Barbera 55 to 70 per cent with Croatina 30 to 45 per cent from the Piacenza hills; a DOC of its own since 2010.
Emilia IGT
The regional IGT, also labelled dell'Emilia, the source of much Lambrusco sold under the family name.

places.name: Modena
places.note: The Lambrusco heart of Emilia, the plain and foothills around the city of balsamic vinegar, holding the three DOCs the Court names.

places.name: Sorbara
places.note: A village on the plain north of Modena between the Secchia and the Panaro, whose sandy alluvium grows the pale, sharp Lambrusco di Sorbara.

places.name: Castelvetro
places.note: A hill town south of Modena at the heart of Lambrusco Grasparossa di Castelvetro, on clay and marl foothills that give a dark, tannic wine.

places.name: Santa Croce
places.note: A village near Carpi, north of Modena, that names Lambrusco Salamino di Santa Croce, the deep, fruity Lambrusco of the plain.

places.name: Reggio Emilia
places.note: The province west of Modena, home of the Reggiano DOC, whose Lambrusco blends often take Ancellotta and come off dry or sweet, and of the large cooperatives behind the export trade.

places.name: Colli di Scandiano e di Canossa
places.note: The hills south of Reggio, a DOC for Lambrusco and for sparkling whites from the local Spergola.

places.name: Colli Piacentini
places.note: The hills south of Piacenza on the Lombard border, a DOC for the white Ortrugo, aromatic Malvasia di Candia and the rare sweet Vin Santo di Vigoleno.

places.name: Gutturnio
places.note: The red of the Piacenza hills, Barbera with Croatina, still or frizzante, with Superiore and Riserva wines; a DOC of its own since 2010.

places.name: Colli di Parma
places.note: The hills south of Parma, the prosciutto country, for frizzante Malvasia and light reds of Barbera and Croatina.

places.name: Colli Bolognesi
places.note: The hills south-west of Bologna, home of the Colli Bolognesi Pignoletto DOCG for Grechetto Gentile whites, still or frizzante. The DOCG was created in 2010 as Colli Bolognesi Classico Pignoletto and renamed in 2014, when a broader Pignoletto DOC was drawn around it; that DOC has been named Emilia-Romagna DOC since the 2024 harvest.

places.name: Romagna
places.note: The eastern half, from Imola to Rimini, where hills of clay, marl and spungone run down towards the Adriatic: Sangiovese for red, Albana and Trebbiano for white.

places.name: The Romagna Sangiovese subzones
places.note: Romagna Sangiovese may name a hill subzone on its label, among them Bertinoro, Brisighella, Modigliana, Predappio, Oriolo and Serra: spungone at Bertinoro and Brisighella, sandstone and marl high in the Apennines at Modigliana.

places.name: Bosco Eliceo
places.note: Sandy coastal land by the Po delta between Ferrara and Ravenna, where Fortana makes a light, sharp and often frizzante red.

producers.name: Cleto Chiarli
producers.why: A Modena house founded in 1860 and a reference for dry Sorbara and Grasparossa, made both in tank and refermented in bottle.

producers.name: Cavicchioli
producers.why: A house of San Prospero in the Sorbara zone, whose Vigna del Cristo is a single vineyard Lambrusco di Sorbara.

producers.name: Paltrinieri
producers.why: A Sorbara family estate whose pale, dry Lambrusco di Sorbara, bottle refermented wines among them, shows the grape's sharp, pale edge.

producers.name: Medici Ermete
producers.why: A Reggio Emilia house whose dry Concerto helped restore the name of dry Reggiano Lambrusco.

producers.name: Cantine Riunite
producers.why: The Reggio Emilia cooperative whose sweet, lightly sparkling Lambrusco became a large seller in the United States from the 1970s.

producers.name: Fattoria Zerbina
producers.why: A Faenza estate whose Scacco Matto, a botrytised Albana passito, makes the case for Albana's DOCG, beside serious Romagna Sangiovese.

producers.name: La Stoppa
producers.why: A historic estate of the Colli Piacentini known for long aged Barbera and Bonarda reds and for Ageno, a skin fermented white led by Malvasia di Candia.

exam: Lambrusco is a family of grapes and of separate DOCs: Sorbara (pale, sharp, at least 60 per cent Sorbara), Grasparossa di Castelvetro (dark, tannic, foothills) and Salamino di Santa Croce (deep, fruity, plain).
Know the sweetness words on a Lambrusco label: secco, amabile and dolce.
Most Lambrusco is made by the tank (Charmat) method, frizzante or spumante; bottle refermentation, the traditional method and the ancestral method also appear.
Romagna Albana was raised in 1987 as the first white DOCG in Italy; it is dry or sweet, the passito from dried grapes.
Romagna's red is Sangiovese, sold as Romagna Sangiovese with Superiore, Riserva and subzone names.
Place the region: it straddles north and central Italy, with the Po to the north, the Apennines to the south and the Adriatic to the east; the Court files it as cool continental.
Serve Lambrusco cold in a flute or a white wine glass with Parmigiano Reggiano, salumi and dishes dressed with balsamic vinegar; an opened bottle loses its sparkle quickly, so watch it by the glass.
traps: There is no single Lambrusco DOC: the Court's subzones are separate DOCs, and much Lambrusco is IGT Emilia.
Dry Lambrusco is the local tradition; the sweet export style is one choice, not the definition.
Lambrusco Mantovano is made in the province of Mantua, in Lombardy, not in Emilia-Romagna.
Albana was the first white DOCG, not the first DOCG: red DOCGs such as Brunello di Montalcino and Barolo came before it.
Pignoletto is Grechetto Gentile, the Grechetto di Todi of Umbria, not the Grechetto of Orvieto.
Gutturnio is a wine, not a grape: a blend of Barbera and Croatina, which the Piacenza hills call Bonarda.
Romagna Sangiovese is a wine of the Adriatic side of the Apennines, not a Tuscan wine, though the grape is shared.

cards.f: Lambrusco: the three DOCs the Court names
cards.b: Lambrusco di Sorbara, Lambrusco Grasparossa di Castelvetro and Lambrusco Salamino di Santa Croce, each a DOC of its own around Modena, all recognised in 1970.

cards.f: Lambrusco di Sorbara: its style and its blend
cards.b: Pale ruby to pink, sharply acidic and floral; at least 60 per cent Sorbara with Salamino for the rest, because Sorbara sets fruit poorly.

cards.f: Lambrusco Grasparossa: the name and the style
cards.b: Graspa is the stalk, which turns red at harvest; grown in the foothills around Castelvetro, it gives dark, full and tannic Lambrusco.

cards.f: Lambrusco: the usual sparkling method
cards.b: The tank method (Charmat or Martinotti), frizzante or spumante; some is refermented in bottle, made by the traditional method or by the ancestral method.

cards.f: Lambrusco: the sweetness words on the label
cards.b: Secco (dry), amabile (medium sweet) and dolce (sweet).

cards.f: Romagna Albana: why it matters
cards.b: Raised in 1987 as Albana di Romagna, the first white DOCG in Italy; secco, amabile, dolce or passito from the Romagna hills.

cards.f: Emilia-Romagna: climate and borders
cards.b: Cool continental by the Court's category; the Po to the north, the Apennines to the south, the Adriatic to the east, straddling north and central Italy.

cards.f: Lambrusco at the table and by the glass
cards.b: Serve it cold in a flute or a white wine glass with Parmigiano Reggiano, salumi and balsamic dishes; an opened bottle loses its sparkle fast.

cards.f: Gutturnio: what is in it?
cards.b: The red of the Piacenza hills: Barbera 55 to 70 per cent with Croatina, called Bonarda there, 30 to 45 per cent; a DOC of its own since 2010.

cards.f: Colli Bolognesi Pignoletto: its grape and its rank
cards.b: A DOCG since 2010 for whites of Grechetto Gentile, called Pignoletto, from the hills south-west of Bologna; still or frizzante.

questions.q: Which Lambrusco DOC asks for only 60 per cent of its own grape, with Salamino making up most of the rest?
questions.exp: Sorbara sets fruit poorly, so its DOC asks at least 60 per cent Sorbara and lets Salamino fill the rest; Grasparossa di Castelvetro asks at least 85 per cent of its grape.

questions.q: Which grape makes Romagna's white DOCG, dry or as a passito?
questions.exp: Albana, a thick skinned native white, was raised to DOCG in 1987 as Albana di Romagna, the first white DOCG in Italy, and is made secco, amabile, dolce or passito.

questions.q: By which sparkling method is most Lambrusco made?
questions.exp: Most Lambrusco takes its second fermentation in a pressure tank, the Charmat or Martinotti method; bottle refermentation, the traditional method and the ancestral method are minority choices, and the transfer method is not used there.

questions.q: Which red grape leads the wines of Romagna?
questions.exp: Romagna's red is Sangiovese, sold as Romagna Sangiovese. Lambrusco Salamino belongs to Emilia, Barbera to the Piacenza hills and Montepulciano to Abruzzo and the Marche.

questions.q: Which label word marks a medium sweet Lambrusco, between secco and dolce?
questions.exp: Lambrusco is labelled secco when dry, amabile when medium sweet and dolce when sweet, the three words the Court lists.

questions.q: Which mountain range forms the southern edge of Emilia-Romagna?
questions.exp: The Apennines run along the south of the region, and the Po along most of its north; the Alps and the Dolomites rise north of the Po, and the Maritime Alps lie on the French border.

questions.q: Which two grapes make Gutturnio, the red of the Piacenza hills?
questions.exp: Gutturnio is Barbera, 55 to 70 per cent, with Croatina, called Bonarda locally, 30 to 45 per cent; it became a DOC of its own in 2010.

questions.q: Which grape, by its variety name, makes the whites of the Colli Bolognesi Pignoletto DOCG?
questions.exp: Pignoletto is Grechetto Gentile, the vine Umbria calls Grechetto di Todi and the Bologna hills also call Alionzina; it is a different variety from the Grechetto of Orvieto.

regions.name: Marche
regions.summary: The Marche, Le Marche in Italian, is the Adriatic face of central Italy: a strip of hills between the Apennines and the sea, south of Emilia-Romagna and north of Abruzzo. Its grape is Verdicchio, a white of high acid and a bitter almond finish, made in the two DOCs the Court names: Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi in the hills behind Ancona and Verdicchio di Matelica in a cooler inland valley. The Riserva of each is a DOCG. Montepulciano leads the reds, nearly alone on the limestone headland of the Conero and blended with Sangiovese in Rosso Piceno, while Pecorino and Passerina are the rising whites of the south.

terroir.climate: The Court files central Italy as maritime on the coast and continental inland, and the Marche shows both within a short drive. The coast and the low hills are warmed by the Adriatic and aired by its breezes, with hot, dry summers and mild winters; inland, under the Apennines, winters are colder, nights cooler and the swing between day and night wider. Matelica, shut off from the sea, is the continental pole of the region, Jesi and the Conero the maritime one.
terroir.soils: Clay and limestone over sandstone and marl cover most of the hills, laid down as seabed and lifted with the Apennines. The Castelli di Jesi hold calcareous clay and sandstone, with sand on some higher ridges; the Matelica valley has more limestone and gravel. The Conero is a block of limestone rising from the sea, and the southern hills around Ascoli and Offida are clay and sand.
terroir.topography: A comb of parallel valleys runs from the Apennine ridge east to the Adriatic, each with its river, so the land rises in a series of hill crests from the coast towards mountains of over 2,000 metres. Monte Conero, south of Ancona, is the one real headland on a long, straight coast. Matelica is the exception to the comb: a valley running north to south between two Apennine ridges, with no opening to the sea.
terroir.water: The rivers are short and parallel: the Esino, whose valley holds the Castelli di Jesi and names the Esino DOC, the Musone, the Potenza, the Chienti, the Tenna and the Tronto on the Abruzzo border. The Adriatic tempers the coast and the lower hills, and the Esino valley carries sea air inland towards Jesi.

grapes.name: Verdicchio
grapes.styles: The region's white, named for its green tinge: high acid, lemon, green almond and a bitter almond finish, and it ages well, gaining honey and nut over a decade or more. DNA ties it to Trebbiano di Soave and to Lugana's Turbiana.

grapes.name: Montepulciano
grapes.styles: The red of the Conero and the base of Rosso Piceno: deep colour, plum and black cherry, soft acid and firm, ripe tannin.

grapes.name: Sangiovese
grapes.styles: Blended with Montepulciano in Rosso Piceno, in Rosso Conero and in many IGT reds, where it adds acid and red cherry fruit.

grapes.name: Pecorino
grapes.styles: A mountain white revived in the south of the region and in Abruzzo: early ripening, high in acid and alcohol, with herbs, citrus and a stony edge; one of the Offida DOCG's whites.

grapes.name: Passerina
grapes.styles: A productive white of the south, fresh and citrusy, made still, sparkling and passito; the second white of the Offida DOCG.

grapes.name: Lacrima
grapes.styles: A red of Morro d'Alba near Ancona, strongly scented of rose and violet, soft and juicy.

grapes.name: Vernaccia Nera
grapes.styles: The red of Serrapetrona, made into a sparkling red from partly dried grapes, dry or sweet.

grapes.name: Bianchello
grapes.styles: Biancame by its variety name, the light, crisp white of the Metauro valley in the north.

wines.style: Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi Classico
wines.note: Straw with green glints, lemon, green apple, fennel and almond, dry and fresh with a bitter almond finish; with brodetto fish soup, fried seafood and crudo.
Riper and longer aged, gaining honey, beeswax and toasted almond over the years; it stands up to white meats, mushrooms and truffle dishes.
Tighter and more mineral than Jesi, with citrus, flint and a saline bite; it opens slowly and repays a few years in bottle.
Montepulciano from the headland, dark and plummy with firm tannin and an earthy, savoury finish; with lamb, game and aged pecorino cheese.
Montepulciano softened by Sangiovese: cherry, plum and dried herbs, medium bodied and ready young; with the stuffed fried olives of Ascoli and grilled meats.
Full and fresh, with sage, citrus and a stony, savoury finish; with grilled fish and young sheep's cheese.
A sparkling red, dry or sweet, with red berries, pepper and a faint bitter edge; the dry version with salumi, the sweet one with dry pastries.
Perfumed with rose, violet and strawberry, soft and juicy; serve it lightly cool with charcuterie or a fish soup.

made.viticulture: Most vineyards sit on hill slopes, trained on Guyot or spurred cordon at moderate density. Verdicchio is vigorous and productive, so quality growers hold back the crop and pick when acid and ripeness balance. The Castelli di Jesi, nearer the sea, ripen earlier than the higher, cooler Matelica valley, where the harvest runs later and the wines keep more acid. Montepulciano ripens late and needs the warm, sunny slopes of the Conero and the south; Pecorino, early ripening, suits the higher sites of the Piceno. The hazards are spring frost in the inland valleys, summer drought and hail, and rain at harvest on the coast.
made.winemaking: Verdicchio is mostly fermented cool in stainless steel and bottled young, but the grape rewards time: many Riserva wines rest on their fine lees for months, some in large old casks and a few in barrique, and they keep for many years. Verdicchio also makes traditional method and tank sparkling wine and a sweet passito. Montepulciano for Conero is macerated for colour and tannin and aged in large casks or barrique, at least two years for the DOCG. Rosso Piceno blends Montepulciano with Sangiovese and ages longer for Superiore. Vernaccia di Serrapetrona is made unusually: part of the grapes is dried for weeks, the fresh grapes are fermented, the must of the dried grapes is added for a second fermentation, and a third fermentation, mostly in pressure tank, makes the sparkle.

law.classification: In 2026 the Marche holds five DOCGs, a longer list of DOCs and the Marche IGT. The Court names the two Verdicchio DOCs, Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi and Verdicchio di Matelica, at least 85 per cent Verdicchio. In 2010 the Riserva of each was raised to DOCG, as Castelli di Jesi Verdicchio Riserva, Jesi's name reordered, and Verdicchio di Matelica Riserva. The Conero DOCG of 2004 is the Riserva level of Rosso Conero, at least 85 per cent Montepulciano. Offida is the DOCG of the south for Pecorino, Passerina and a Montepulciano led red, and Vernaccia di Serrapetrona the DOCG of a sparkling red. Among the DOCs, Rosso Piceno blends Montepulciano with Sangiovese, and Lacrima di Morro d'Alba is a scented red. On the labels, Classico marks the historic core of the Jesi zone, Superiore a higher minimum alcohol and Riserva longer ageing.
tiers: Castelli di Jesi Verdicchio Riserva DOCG
Verdicchio Riserva from the Jesi hills, raised to DOCG in 2010; Classico from the historic core.
Verdicchio di Matelica Riserva DOCG
Verdicchio Riserva from the inland Matelica valley, raised to DOCG in 2010.
Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi DOC
At least 85 per cent Verdicchio from the larger zone in the hills west of Ancona; Classico, Superiore, spumante and passito.
Verdicchio di Matelica DOC
At least 85 per cent Verdicchio from the north to south valley around Matelica.
Conero DOCG
The Riserva level of Rosso Conero, raised in 2004: at least 85 per cent Montepulciano, up to 15 per cent Sangiovese, two years of ageing.
Rosso Conero DOC
The younger Montepulciano led red of the headland south of Ancona.
Offida DOCG
Pecorino, Passerina and a Montepulciano led Rosso from the hills around Offida in the south.
Vernaccia di Serrapetrona DOCG
A sparkling red of Vernaccia Nera, part of it dried, dry or sweet.

Montepulciano 35 to 85 per cent with Sangiovese 15 to 50 per cent; Superiore from a smaller southern area near Ascoli.
Lacrima di Morro d'Alba DOC
At least 85 per cent Lacrima from the hills around Morro d'Alba, north-west of Ancona.
Marche IGT
The regional IGT for wines outside the DOC rules.

places.name: Castelli di Jesi
places.note: The hills west of Ancona on both banks of the Esino, named for the walled hill towns, the castelli, around Jesi: the larger Verdicchio zone, nearer the sea, with Classico covering its historic core.

places.name: Cupramontana and Staffolo
places.note: Hill towns on the higher right bank of the Esino, among the zone's cooler sites, whose Verdicchio is taut and slow to age.

places.name: Matelica
places.note: A high inland valley in the Apennines, running north to south between two ridges and closed to the sea, so its climate is continental with cold nights; its Verdicchio is leaner, sharper and slower to open than Jesi's.

places.name: Conero
places.note: Monte Conero, a limestone headland rising straight from the Adriatic south of Ancona, whose slopes grow Montepulciano for Rosso Conero and the Conero DOCG.

places.name: Piceno
places.note: The hills of the south around Ascoli Piceno, home of Rosso Piceno, a blend of Montepulciano and Sangiovese, with its Superiore from a smaller area near Ascoli.

places.name: Offida
places.note: A hill town north of Ascoli whose DOCG covers Pecorino, Passerina and a Montepulciano led Rosso.

places.name: Morro d'Alba
places.note: A village in the hills north-west of Ancona, home of the scented red Lacrima di Morro d'Alba.

places.name: Serrapetrona
places.note: A hill village in the province of Macerata whose DOCG makes Vernaccia Nera into a sparkling red, dry or sweet, by three fermentations.

places.name: Bianchello del Metauro
places.note: The Metauro valley inland from Fano in the north of the region, a DOC for the light white Bianchello, Biancame by its variety name.

producers.name: Bucci
producers.why: A Castelli di Jesi estate whose Villa Bucci Riserva, matured in large old casks, makes the case for Verdicchio as a white to age.

producers.name: La Monacesca
producers.why: A Matelica estate whose Mirum Riserva shows the tighter, slower inland Verdicchio.

producers.name: Fazi Battaglia
producers.why: A Castelli di Jesi house whose amphora shaped bottle carried Verdicchio abroad in the decades after the Second World War.

producers.name: Garofoli
producers.why: An old family house of Loreto known for Verdicchio, sparkling wines among them, and for Grosso Agontano, a Conero Riserva.

producers.name: Saladini Pilastri
producers.why: An old family estate of the Piceno, farmed organically, known for Rosso Piceno Superiore and Offida Pecorino.

producers.name: Velenosi
producers.why: An Ascoli Piceno house known for Rosso Piceno Superiore and for the Offida whites, Pecorino and Passerina.

exam: Verdicchio is the Marche's grape: name the two DOCs the Court lists, Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi and Verdicchio di Matelica, and know that the Riserva of each became a DOCG in 2010.
Tell the zones apart: Castelli di Jesi in the hills west of Ancona, open to the sea; Matelica in a high inland valley running north to south, cooler and continental.
Verdicchio is the same variety as Trebbiano di Soave and so close to Lugana's Turbiana in DNA studies that the two are often taught as one; no relation of Trebbiano Toscano.
Montepulciano leads the reds: Rosso Conero and the Conero DOCG on the limestone headland, Rosso Piceno blended with Sangiovese.
Climate: maritime on the coast and continental inland, the Court's category for central Italy; the Apennines to the west and the Adriatic to the east.
Superiore on a label means a higher minimum alcohol; Riserva means longer ageing.
From Premier Cru, know Offida for Pecorino and Passerina, and Vernaccia di Serrapetrona as a sparkling red.
traps: Montepulciano here is the grape, as in Abruzzo; Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is Sangiovese from a Tuscan town.
The Court lists the Verdicchio zones as DOCs; the DOCG belongs only to the Riserva wines, named Castelli di Jesi Verdicchio Riserva and Verdicchio di Matelica Riserva.
Matelica is the smaller, higher and inland zone; Castelli di Jesi is the larger one, nearer the sea.
Vernaccia di Serrapetrona is a red sparkling wine from Vernaccia Nera, unrelated to the white Vernaccia di San Gimignano of Tuscany.
Pecorino is a white grape of the Marche and Abruzzo as well as a sheep's cheese.
Lacrima di Morro d'Alba is a red of the Marche, nothing to do with Alba in Piedmont.
The Conero DOCG is the Riserva level; plain Rosso Conero stays a DOC.

cards.f: Marche: the two Verdicchio DOCs the Court names
cards.b: Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi, in the hills west of Ancona, and Verdicchio di Matelica, in a high inland valley; the Riserva of each became a DOCG in 2010.

cards.f: Matelica against Castelli di Jesi
cards.b: Matelica: smaller, higher, inland, a north to south valley closed to the sea, continental, leaner and slower to open. Jesi: larger, nearer the sea, broader.

cards.f: Verdicchio: its identity by DNA
cards.b: The same variety as Trebbiano di Soave in the Veneto, and so close to Turbiana at Lugana that it is often taught as the same vine; no relation of Trebbiano Toscano.

cards.f: Verdicchio: how does it taste?
cards.b: Lemon, green apple, fennel and almond, high acid and a bitter almond finish; Riserva wines gain honey and toasted almond with age.

cards.f: Conero DOCG: the grape and the rule
cards.b: The Riserva level of Rosso Conero, a DOCG since 2004: at least 85 per cent Montepulciano, up to 15 per cent Sangiovese, two years of ageing.

cards.f: Rosso Piceno: the blend
cards.b: Montepulciano 35 to 85 per cent with Sangiovese 15 to 50 per cent, from the southern hills; Superiore from a smaller area near Ascoli.

cards.f: Marche: climate and physical features
cards.b: Maritime on the Adriatic coast, continental inland under the Apennines; parallel river valleys run from the mountains to the sea, broken by the Conero headland.

cards.f: Offida DOCG: its three wines
cards.b: Pecorino, Passerina and a Montepulciano led Rosso, from the hills of the Piceno in the south.

cards.f: Vernaccia di Serrapetrona: what is it?
cards.b: A DOCG sparkling red from Vernaccia Nera, part of the grapes dried, made by three fermentations and sold dry or sweet.

cards.f: Lacrima di Morro d'Alba: grape and style
cards.b: A red of at least 85 per cent Lacrima from the hills near Ancona, scented with rose and violet, soft and juicy.

questions.q: Which Marche zone grows Verdicchio in an inland valley running north to south, closed to the sea?
questions.exp: Matelica's valley runs north to south between Apennine ridges, so it is cooler and continental; the Castelli di Jesi open towards the sea, the Conero grows Montepulciano and Offida lies in the south.

questions.q: Which red grape leads the Conero DOCG?
questions.exp: Conero, the Riserva level of Rosso Conero, takes at least 85 per cent Montepulciano with up to 15 per cent Sangiovese; the grape shares its name with a Tuscan town whose wine is Sangiovese.

questions.q: Which grape is blended with Montepulciano in Rosso Piceno?
questions.exp: Rosso Piceno takes Montepulciano with 15 to 50 per cent Sangiovese. Lacrima makes its own DOC at Morro d'Alba, Aglianico belongs to Campania and Basilicata, and Cabernet Sauvignon appears in Marche IGT blends.

questions.q: In which year were the Verdicchio Riserva wines of Jesi and Matelica raised to DOCG?
questions.exp: Both Riservas became DOCGs in 2010, as Castelli di Jesi Verdicchio Riserva and Verdicchio di Matelica Riserva; 2004 is the year of the Conero DOCG.

questions.q: Which label word on a Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi marks wine from the historic core of the zone?
accept: Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi Classico
questions.exp: Classico marks the historic heart of the Jesi zone; Superiore marks a higher minimum alcohol and Riserva longer ageing, the Riserva carrying the DOCG.

questions.q: Which sea shapes the coastal climate of the Marche?
questions.exp: The Marche faces the Adriatic, which tempers its coast and low hills; the Tyrrhenian and Ligurian seas wash the west coast of Italy and the Ionian the south.

questions.q: Which grape makes the sparkling red DOCG of Serrapetrona?
questions.exp: Vernaccia di Serrapetrona is made from Vernaccia Nera, part of it dried, by three fermentations. Lacrima and Montepulciano are other Marche reds, and Cesanese Comune belongs to Lazio.

questions.q: Which red grape, scented of rose and violet, makes the DOC wine of Morro d'Alba?
questions.exp: Lacrima di Morro d'Alba takes at least 85 per cent Lacrima, a soft, intensely perfumed red grape of the hills north-west of Ancona.

regions.name: Liguria and Valle d'Aosta
regions.summary: Two small regions of Italy's north-west, read together. Liguria is the narrow arc of coast around Genoa, where the Maritime Alps and the Apennines fall straight into the Ligurian Sea and vines cling to terraces: Vermentino and Pigato make saline whites, Rossese di Dolceacqua a pale, perfumed red, and the Cinque Terre a dry white and the sweet Sciacchetrà from dried grapes. Beyond Piedmont to the north, the Valle d'Aosta is Italy's smallest wine region, an Alpine valley under Mont Blanc with one regional DOC, seven named sub-zones and grapes found almost nowhere else: Petit Rouge, Fumin, Prié Blanc and Petite Arvine, with Nebbiolo in the lower valley.

terroir.climate: Liguria is Mediterranean: mild winters, warm, dry summers and constant sea breezes, with the mountains at its back shutting out the cold north winds, so olives and vines share the same slopes. Rain falls mostly in autumn and can come in violent storms. The Valle d'Aosta is Alpine and continental, but the high peaks around it hold off much of the rain, so it is dry and sunny for a mountain valley, with cold winters, warm days and cool nights in summer. The wide swing from day to night keeps acidity and aroma in the grapes; spring frost and an early autumn are the hazards.
terroir.soils: Liguria's terraces are cut into poor, stony ground, mostly schist, sandstone and marl, with clay and limestone in places, built up behind dry stone walls and quick to drain. The Valle d'Aosta's vineyards lie on glacial moraine and the debris of old rockfalls over crystalline rock: sandy, stony, thin soils low in organic matter that warm quickly in the sun and drain freely.
terroir.topography: Liguria is a strip only a few kilometres deep in places, curving from the French border to Tuscany with Genoa at its centre: the Riviera di Ponente runs west of the city, the Riviera di Levante east. Slopes rise straight from the sea to the ridges, so almost every vineyard is terraced, at the Cinque Terre on cliffs above the water. The Valle d'Aosta runs east from Mont Blanc along the Dora Baltea to the narrow gap at Pont-Saint-Martin, where it opens into Piedmont. Vines grow mostly on the south-facing slopes of the valley's north side, on terraces from the valley floor up to about 1,200 metres at Morgex.
terroir.water: The Ligurian Sea, the north-western arm of the Mediterranean, warms the coast in winter and cools it in summer, and its breezes dry the vines after rain. The Dora Baltea drains the Valle d'Aosta from the glaciers of Mont Blanc east into Piedmont and on to the Po, and the cold air that slides down from the ice at night keeps the upper valley fresh.

grapes.name: Vermentino
grapes.styles: The main white of both Rivieras and of the Colli di Luni: citrus, herbs and a saline finish, mostly unoaked and drunk young.

grapes.name: Pigato
grapes.styles: Vermentino by DNA, grown as a separate vine with freckled skins on the Riviera di Ponente around Albenga; fuller and more savoury than the coast's Vermentino.

grapes.name: Bosco
grapes.styles: The lead white of the Cinque Terre, with Albarola and Vermentino, the backbone of both the dry white and the sweet Sciacchetrà.

grapes.name: Albarola
grapes.styles: A Cinque Terre and Levante white, the partner of Bosco, light and fresh.

grapes.name: Rossese
grapes.styles: The grape of Rossese di Dolceacqua in the far west, the same vine as Provence's Tibouren: pale, perfumed reds of red berries, roses and spice.

grapes.name: Dolcetto
grapes.styles: Called Ormeasco in the hills of Pornassio, where it makes a firm red and a rosé called Sciac-trà.

grapes.name: Petit Rouge
grapes.styles: The Valle d'Aosta's main red, behind Torrette and Enfer d'Arvier: light to medium bodied, with cherries, violets and a bitter almond finish.

grapes.name: Fumin
grapes.styles: A darker, firmer native red, peppery and structured, bottled alone and often aged in wood, or blended with Petit Rouge.

grapes.name: Nebbiolo
grapes.styles: Called Picotendro or Picotener in the lower valley, where it makes Donnas and Arnad-Montjovet: paler and leaner than Barolo, with rose and red cherry.

grapes.name: Prié Blanc
grapes.styles: The only grape of Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle, grown ungrafted under Mont Blanc: very light, crisp and herbal, still or sparkling.

grapes.name: Petite Arvine
grapes.styles: Shared with the Swiss Valais: a saline, high-acid white of grapefruit and herbs, increasingly planted in the valley.

grapes.name: Cornalin
grapes.styles: A native red of the valley, the vine the Valais calls Humagne Rouge, deep in colour and spicy.

grapes.name: Muscat Blanc
grapes.styles: Moscato Bianco at Chambave, made dry and as the sweet Flétri from grapes dried after picking.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Called Malvoisie at Nus, made dry or sweet from dried grapes, with a coppery tint.

wines.note: Dry and saline, from Bosco, Albarola and Vermentino grown on the sea cliffs: lemon, herbs and a salty finish. Pour it with anchovies, pesto and the fish of the Ligurian coast.
Amber and sweet, from dried Bosco, Albarola and Vermentino: apricot, honey, dried figs and a bitter orange edge, sold in small bottles. Serve it with blue cheese or almond biscuits.
Fuller than Vermentino, with peach, herbs, a hint of bitter almond and a saline finish; a match for pesto, focaccia and grilled fish.
Pale, fragrant and soft, with wild strawberry, rose and white pepper. Serve it cool with rabbit, the Ligurian classic, or with a fish soup.
Light to medium bodied Petit Rouge: cherries, violets and almond with fresh acidity, for fontina, cured meats and polenta.

wines.style: Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle
wines.note: Very pale, light and crisp, with mountain herbs, green apple and a mineral, saline edge; also made sparkling. An aperitif, or a glass with trout.
Saline, with grapefruit and rhubarb, brisk acidity and more weight than Prié Blanc; for fondue or freshwater fish.
Nebbiolo from the lower valley: pale, with rose and red cherry and firm, fine tannin, lighter than Barolo; for game birds and mountain cheese.
A Moscato from dried grapes: honeyed, with apricot and orange peel and the acidity of the mountains to balance its sweetness.

made.viticulture: Both regions are farmed by hand on steep ground. In Liguria the vineyards stand on terraces held up by dry stone walls built over centuries, and many were abandoned in the twentieth century as the coast's other work paid better. At the Cinque Terre small monorail trains carry grapes and tools up and down the cliffs, and vines are kept low, on short pergolas or as bush vines, out of the wind. Yields are small and costs high. In the Valle d'Aosta the vines climb terraces on the sunny north side of the valley. At Morgex and La Salle, Prié Blanc grows ungrafted on low pergolas close to the ground, which take the warmth the stony soil stores by day through the cold nights; phylloxera never took hold at that height, and new vines are still propagated on their own roots. Lower down, at Donnas, Nebbiolo is trained on pergolas held up by stone pillars, as at Carema across the border in Piedmont. Frost, a short season and the steepness of the ground keep every harvest small.
made.winemaking: Most whites in both regions are fermented cool in steel and bottled young to keep their freshness and salinity; some Pigato and Vermentino is kept on its lees or rested in large wood for texture. Sciacchetrà is made from the ripest bunches of Bosco, Albarola and Vermentino, dried for weeks in airy lofts or on racks until the berries shrivel, then pressed late in the autumn and fermented slowly into a sweet, amber wine. In the Valle d'Aosta, Petit Rouge is made for freshness and drunk within a few years, while Fumin and Donnas take longer and often see wood. Chambave Muscat and Nus Malvoisie are also made as Flétri, the valley's French word for a wine from grapes dried after picking. Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle is made still and as a sparkling wine, including by the traditional method. Cooperatives make much of the valley's wine and keep its many small growers in business.

law.classification: Liguria has no DOCG. Its wines are DOC or IGT: Rossese di Dolceacqua became the region's first DOC in 1972, and Cinque Terre, with Cinque Terre Sciacchetrà, followed in 1973. Riviera Ligure di Ponente is the broad DOC of the western coast, for Pigato, Vermentino, Rossese and others, and Ormeasco di Pornassio was split from it as a DOC of its own in 2003. In the east, Colli di Luni crosses the border into Tuscany, and Golfo del Tigullio-Portofino, Colline di Levanto and Val Polcevera cover the hills of the Levante and around Genoa. The Valle d'Aosta has a single DOC, Valle d'Aosta or Vallée d'Aoste, written in Italian or French, which absorbed the older Donnas and Enfer d'Arvier DOCs. Its label carries the regional name with a grape, such as Petite Arvine or Fumin, or with one of seven named sub-zones. Like Piedmont next door, the Valle d'Aosta has never registered an IGT.

places.name: Riviera di Ponente
places.note: The coast west of Genoa to the French border, warmer and drier than the east, home of Pigato, Vermentino and Rossese under the broad Riviera Ligure di Ponente DOC.

places.name: Rossese di Dolceacqua
places.note: The valleys of the Nervia and its neighbours behind Ventimiglia, around the village of Dolceacqua near the French border: pale, perfumed Rossese reds, Liguria's first DOC in 1972.

places.name: Albenga
places.note: The plain and hills around Albenga in Savona province, the heartland of Pigato, whose wines are fuller and more savoury than the coast's Vermentino.

places.name: Ormeasco di Pornassio
places.note: High hills of the upper Arroscia valley in Imperia province, towards Piedmont, where Dolcetto is called Ormeasco and makes a red and the rosé Sciac-trà; a DOC of its own since 2003.

places.name: Riviera di Levante
places.note: The coast east of Genoa to Tuscany, steeper and more rugged, with Vermentino, Bosco, Albarola and Bianchetta Genovese on terraces above the sea.

places.name: Cinque Terre
places.note: Five villages on the cliffs north-west of La Spezia, Monterosso al Mare, Vernazza, Corniglia, Manarola and Riomaggiore, with terraced vineyards over the sea, worked by hand and by monorail: the dry white and the sweet Sciacchetrà.

places.name: Colli di Luni
places.note: The hills around the old Roman port of Luni at Liguria's eastern end, a DOC that crosses into Tuscany, known for full, saline Vermentino.

places.name: Golfo del Tigullio-Portofino and Colline di Levanto
places.note: Two small DOCs of the Levante hills between Genoa and the Cinque Terre, for Vermentino, Bianchetta Genovese and Ciliegiolo.

places.name: Valle d'Aosta
places.note: The Alpine valley of the Dora Baltea between Mont Blanc and Piedmont, Italy's smallest wine region, with one DOC and seven named sub-zones on the sunny north side of the valley.

places.name: Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle
places.note: The upper valley under Mont Blanc, from about 900 to 1,200 metres: ungrafted Prié Blanc on low pergolas, still or sparkling.

places.name: Enfer d'Arvier
places.note: A hot, sheltered bowl of rock at Arvier west of Aosta, whose name means hell for its summer heat; reds of Petit Rouge, once a DOC of its own.

places.name: Torrette
places.note: The communes either side of the city of Aosta, on the sunny slopes of the central valley, for reds led by Petit Rouge.

places.name: Nus
places.note: East of Aosta, for a red of the local Vien de Nus and for Malvoisie, the local name for Pinot Gris, dry or Flétri.

places.name: Chambave
places.note: The middle valley east of Nus, known for Moscato Bianco made dry and as the sweet Flétri, and for a red of Petit Rouge.

places.name: Arnad-Montjovet
places.note: The lower valley below Saint-Vincent, where Nebbiolo begins to lead the reds, as it does at Donnas.

places.name: Donnas
places.note: The last sub-zone before Piedmont, at the mouth of the valley: Nebbiolo, called Picotendro, on terraces and stone-pillared pergolas, once a DOC of its own.

producers.name: Cantina Cinque Terre
producers.why: The growers' cooperative at Groppo above Manarola, which gathers grapes from many small terraces into the dry Cinque Terre white and Sciacchetrà.

producers.name: Bisson
producers.why: A Chiavari house of the Riviera di Levante, known for Vermentino, Bianchetta Genovese and Cinque Terre wines.

producers.name: Terre Bianche
producers.why: A Dolceacqua estate, a reference for Rossese di Dolceacqua and for Pigato from the western coast.

producers.name: Lunae
producers.why: An estate of the Colli di Luni on the Tuscan border, a reference for Vermentino.

producers.name: Cave Mont Blanc de Morgex et La Salle
producers.why: The cooperative of the upper valley, the main source of Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle, still and sparkling.

producers.name: Caves Coopératives de Donnas
producers.why: The cooperative of the lower valley, the main source of Donnas Nebbiolo from the stone-pillared terraces.

producers.name: Institut Agricole Régional
producers.why: The Aosta agricultural school and research centre, which studies the valley's native grapes and bottles wines from them.

producers.name: Les Crêtes
producers.why: An Aymavilles estate known for Petite Arvine, Fumin and Chardonnay.

producers.name: La Crotta di Vegneron
producers.why: The Chambave cooperative, known for Chambave Muscat and its Flétri and for Nus Malvoisie.

exam: Place both regions: Liguria on the coast around Genoa between France and Tuscany, the Valle d'Aosta in the Alps under Mont Blanc, north of Piedmont.
Know Vermentino as the lead white of the Ligurian coast and Pigato as Vermentino by DNA, bottled under its own name.
Know Sciacchetrà as the Cinque Terre's sweet wine from dried Bosco, Albarola and Vermentino, and the Cinque Terre as terraces on cliffs above the sea.
Know Rossese di Dolceacqua as a pale red of the far west and Liguria's first DOC, in 1972; Liguria has no DOCG.
Know the Valle d'Aosta as Italy's smallest wine region, with one DOC, Valle d'Aosta or Vallée d'Aoste, and no IGT.
Name the valley's grapes: Petit Rouge and Fumin red, Prié Blanc and Petite Arvine white, and Nebbiolo called Picotendro at Donnas, on stone-pillared pergolas like Carema's over the Piedmont border.
Know Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle: Prié Blanc, ungrafted, on low pergolas at up to about 1,200 metres.
The seven sub-zones and Ormeasco as Dolcetto are asked from Premier Cru; Golfo del Tigullio-Portofino and Colline di Levanto from Grand Cru.
traps: Pigato and Vermentino are one variety by DNA, though they are grown and bottled under separate names.
Sciacchetrà is the Cinque Terre's sweet passito; Sciac-trà is the dry rosé of Ormeasco di Pornassio.
Ormeasco is Dolcetto, not a separate grape.
Liguria has no DOCG; the Valle d'Aosta has one DOC and no IGT.
The Valle d'Aosta's Cornalin is the Valais's Humagne Rouge, not the Valais's own Cornalin.
Donnas and Carema both grow Nebbiolo on stone pillars, but Carema is in Piedmont, not the Valle d'Aosta.
Malvoisie at Nus is Pinot Gris, not a Malvasia.
Colli di Luni crosses the regional border: part of it lies in Tuscany.

cards.b: One regional DOC, Valle d'Aosta or Vallée d'Aoste, labelled with a grape or a named sub-zone; no DOCG and no IGT.

cards.f: Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle: grape and vineyard
cards.b: Prié Blanc, grown ungrafted on low pergolas under Mont Blanc at up to about 1,200 metres; light, crisp and herbal, still or sparkling.

cards.f: Nebbiolo in the Valle d'Aosta: its name and its sub-zones
cards.b: Picotendro, or Picotener; it makes Donnas and Arnad-Montjovet in the lower valley, paler and leaner than Barolo.

cards.f: Petite Arvine: where else it grows and its style
cards.b: Over the pass in the Swiss Valais. In the Valle d'Aosta it makes a saline, high-acid white of grapefruit and herbs.

cards.f: Ormeasco: its identity and its rosé
cards.b: Dolcetto, in the hills of Pornassio in Imperia province. Its rosé is called Sciac-trà, a dry wine, not the Cinque Terre's sweet Sciacchetrà.

cards.f: The Valle d'Aosta's seven sub-zones, upstream to downstream
cards.b: Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle, Enfer d'Arvier, Torrette, Nus, Chambave, Arnad-Montjovet and Donnas.

cards.f: Donnas and Carema: what they share
cards.b: Nebbiolo trained on pergolas held up by stone pillars, on terraces either side of the border where the Valle d'Aosta opens into Piedmont.

questions.q: Which white grape has DNA profiling shown to be the same variety as Liguria's Pigato?
questions.exp: Pigato is Vermentino, grown on the Riviera di Ponente as a separate vine with freckled skins. Bosco and Albarola are the Cinque Terre's own whites, and Trebbiano Toscano is a partner in some Levante blends.

questions.q: What is the sweet wine made from dried grapes on the terraces of the Cinque Terre called?
questions.exp: Sciacchetrà is made from Bosco, Albarola and Vermentino dried for weeks after picking, then pressed and fermented into an amber, sweet wine sold in small bottles.

questions.q: Which Ligurian denomination became the region's first DOC, in 1972?
questions.exp: Rossese di Dolceacqua, behind Ventimiglia, was granted in 1972. Cinque Terre followed in 1973, while Colli di Luni and Riviera Ligure di Ponente came later.

questions.q: Which white grape grows ungrafted on low pergolas for Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle?
questions.exp: Prié Blanc is the only grape of Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle, grown on its own roots under Mont Blanc. Petite Arvine, Chardonnay and Müller-Thurgau are grown lower in the valley.

questions.q: What is Nebbiolo called in the lower Valle d'Aosta, where it makes Donnas?
questions.exp: In the Valle d'Aosta Nebbiolo is Picotendro or Picotener, as at Carema over the border; it is Spanna in Alto Piemonte and Chiavennasca in Valtellina.

questions.q: How many named sub-zones does the Valle d'Aosta DOC hold?
questions.exp: Seven: Blanc de Morgex et de La Salle, Enfer d'Arvier, Torrette, Nus, Chambave, Arnad-Montjovet and Donnas, from Mont Blanc down to the Piedmont border.

questions.q: Which grape is called Ormeasco in the hills of Pornassio?
questions.exp: Ormeasco is Dolcetto, which crossed from Piedmont into the hills of Imperia province. Rossese is the grape of Dolceacqua, and Barbera and Nebbiolo stay mostly in Piedmont.

questions.q: Which Piedmontese denomination shares Donnas's Nebbiolo trained on stone-pillared pergolas?
questions.exp: Carema lies just over the Piedmont border from Donnas, and both train Nebbiolo on pergolas resting on stone pillars on steep terraces.

regions.name: Lazio
regions.summary: Lazio is the region of Rome, on the Tyrrhenian coast of central Italy between Tuscany and Campania, with the Apennines along its eastern side. It is volcanic country: crater lakes and old ash and tuff run from Lake Bolsena in the north to the Alban Hills just south-east of the city. Its wine to know is Frascati, the Malvasia led white of the Castelli Romani hills, a DOC since 1966, whose Superiore and sweet Cannellino became DOCGs in 2011. Cesanese del Piglio, from the native Cesanese, is the region's red DOCG, and Est! Est!! Est!!! di Montefiascone, on Lake Bolsena, is the white with the legend.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean on the coast: hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters, with breezes off the Tyrrhenian Sea. The Court files central Italy as maritime on the coast and continental inland, and Lazio's inland hills under the Apennines, around Piglio and Olevano Romano, have colder winters and cooler nights than Rome's plain. The crater lakes temper the hills around them, and drought in hot summers is the growing hazard.
terroir.soils: Volcanic above all. Four main volcanic districts, the Vulsini around Lake Bolsena, the Cimini around Lake Vico, the Sabatini around Lake Bracciano and the Alban Hills south-east of Rome, left ash, tuff and lava that weather into light, porous soils rich in potassium. Inland, the Piglio hills mix volcanic material with red clay and limestone, and the coastal plains south of Rome are sand and reclaimed marsh.
terroir.topography: A coastal plain along the Tyrrhenian, the Roman Campagna, rises inland to volcanic hills ringed with crater lakes and then to the limestone ridges of the Apennines. The Castelli Romani are the hill towns on the rim of the old Alban volcano, looking down on Rome from the south-east. The north, called Tuscia, is a tuff plateau around Lake Bolsena; the south-east, the Ciociaria around Frosinone, is a land of hills below the Ernici mountains.
terroir.water: The Tiber crosses the region to the sea near Ostia. The crater lakes, Bolsena, Vico, Bracciano, Albano and Nemi, soften the extremes on their shores, and the Tyrrhenian moderates the coast and the reclaimed plain of the Agro Pontino.

grapes.name: Malvasia del Lazio
grapes.styles: Also called Malvasia Puntinata for the dots on its berries: the scented quality white of Frascati and the Castelli Romani, with peach, apricot and a soft, full texture.

grapes.name: Malvasia Bianca di Candia
grapes.styles: The more widely planted Malvasia of the region, productive and less aromatic, the bulk of many Frascati blends beside Malvasia del Lazio.

grapes.name: Trebbiano Toscano
grapes.styles: Called Procanico around Montefiascone, where it leads Est! Est!! Est!!!; elsewhere it adds neutral freshness to Malvasia.

grapes.name: Bellone
grapes.styles: An old local white revived on the coast around Anzio and Nettuno and in the Castelli Romani: citrus, herbs and a saline finish.

grapes.name: Cesanese
grapes.styles: Lazio's native red, from two vines, the small berried Cesanese di Affile and Cesanese Comune: medium bodied, perfumed with cherry, violet and pepper, with a faint bitter finish.

grapes.name: Montepulciano
grapes.styles: The base of the Roma DOC's red, at least half its blend, beside Cesanese and international grapes.

grapes.name: Aleatico
grapes.styles: A scented red relation of Muscat, made into sweet red wine at Gradoli on Lake Bolsena.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Widely planted for the Lazio IGT reds, from the hills of Montefiascone to the coastal plain south of Rome.

wines.note: Dry, light and fresh, with pear, almond and a touch of Malvasia's peach: the everyday white of Rome's trattorie, with fried artichokes, saltimbocca and cacio e pepe.
Riper and fuller, with more of the Malvasia's apricot and a longer, savoury finish; with porchetta, white meats and fish baked in salt.
Golden and sweet from late picked grapes, with honey, apricot and almond; with the ciambelline and dry pastries of the Castelli.
Medium bodied, perfumed with sour cherry, violet and pepper, fresh in acid with a gentle bitter finish; with abbacchio, the Roman milk fed lamb, and pasta all'amatriciana.
Light, dry or off dry, with green apple and almond; a lakeside white for fish from Lake Bolsena.
A sweet red scented with rose and raspberry, still or fortified as a liquoroso; with dark chocolate and berry tarts.
Montepulciano led, with Cesanese and international grapes: dark fruit, soft tannin and a medium to full body, for grilled meats and Roman offal dishes.

made.viticulture: The Castelli Romani supplied Rome with wine for centuries, and the bulk trade of the twentieth century brought high trellises and large crops that thinned Frascati's name. Growers seeking quality have since lowered yields, planted more Malvasia del Lazio and returned to the better slopes. Volcanic soils drain fast and hold warmth, so summer drought is a growing hazard, with hail and the humidity that brings mildew. Cesanese ripens late in the cooler hills of the Piglio and is picked in October. On the Agro Pontino, the coastal plain south of Rome reclaimed from marsh in the 1930s, vineyards are flat, trellised and productive.
made.winemaking: Frascati is fermented cool in stainless steel and bottled young; the better producers give Malvasia del Lazio a short skin contact or months on its fine lees for texture, and Frascati Superiore may age as a Riserva. Cannellino di Frascati comes from grapes left on the vine to concentrate, sometimes touched by noble rot, and its fermentation stops with sugar left in the wine. Cesanese is fermented with moderate extraction to keep its perfume and aged in large casks or barrique for the Superiore and Riserva wines. Est! Est!! Est!!! is a cool fermented white, dry or off dry. Aleatico di Gradoli is made sweet, and as a liquoroso fortified with spirit. Across the region, the Lazio IGT covers international grapes from Merlot to Petit Verdot, made in a modern style.

law.classification: In 2026 Lazio holds three DOCGs, a long list of DOCs, many of them small, and the regional Lazio IGT. Cesanese del Piglio, raised in 2008, is the red DOCG. Frascati Superiore and Cannellino di Frascati, both raised in 2011, were carved from the Frascati DOC of 1966, one of Italy's early DOCs, and take at least 70 per cent Malvasia, Bianca di Candia or del Lazio. Est! Est!! Est!!! di Montefiascone, also a DOC of 1966, is led by Trebbiano Toscano. The Roma DOC, created in 2011, covers the province of Rome, its red at least half Montepulciano, its white led by Malvasia del Lazio. Other DOCs include Castelli Romani, Marino, Cesanese di Olevano Romano, Cesanese di Affile, Aleatico di Gradoli and the Lazio side of Orvieto. Superiore marks a riper wine with higher minimum alcohol, Riserva longer ageing.

places.name: Castelli Romani
places.note: The ring of hill towns on the rim of the old Alban volcano, around Lakes Albano and Nemi just south-east of Rome, on light, porous volcanic soil: Rome's own vineyard for centuries, with a regional Castelli Romani DOC beside the town DOCs.

places.name: Frascati
places.note: The town that names the Castelli's white, a DOC since 1966; Frascati Superiore and Cannellino di Frascati became DOCGs in 2011, the Cannellino zone taking in Frascati, Grottaferrata, Monte Porzio Catone and parts of Monte Compatri and Rome.

places.name: Marino
places.note: A Castelli town above Lake Albano with a DOC of its own for Malvasia led whites.

places.name: Montefiascone and Lake Bolsena
places.note: A hill town on the rim of the Bolsena crater in the north, home of Est! Est!! Est!!! di Montefiascone, a Procanico led white named for a tale of a bishop's servant who marked the inns where the wine was good.

places.name: Gradoli
places.note: A village above the north-western shore of Lake Bolsena whose DOC makes sweet red Aleatico, still or fortified.

places.name: Piglio
places.note: Hills in the province of Frosinone, south-east of Rome below the Ernici mountains, where Cesanese del Piglio, the red DOCG of 2008, grows on volcanic soil, red clay and limestone.

places.name: Olevano Romano and Affile
places.note: Hill towns north-west of Piglio with Cesanese DOCs of their own; Affile gives its name to the small berried Cesanese di Affile vine.

places.name: Roma
places.note: The Roma DOC of 2011 covers the province of Rome, for Montepulciano led reds and rosés and whites led by Malvasia del Lazio.

places.name: Orvieto in Lazio
places.note: The Orvieto DOC crosses from Umbria into the province of Viterbo; its Lazio side grows the same Grechetto and Procanico whites, taught under Umbria.

places.name: Agro Pontino
places.note: The coastal plain south of Rome around Latina, reclaimed from marsh in the 1930s, a source of international reds and of revived Bellone near Anzio and Nettuno.

producers.name: Fontana Candida
producers.why: A Frascati house whose wines carried Frascati to export markets, with the single vineyard Santa Teresa as its reference Frascati Superiore.

producers.name: Castel de Paolis
producers.why: A Grottaferrata estate that led the revival of quality Frascati from the 1980s, with whites built on Malvasia del Lazio.

producers.name: Principe Pallavicini
producers.why: A noble estate of the Castelli Romani known for Frascati and for varietal Malvasia Puntinata under the Roma DOC.

producers.name: Casale della Ioria
producers.why: A family estate at Acuto in the Piglio zone known for Cesanese del Piglio.

producers.name: Falesco
producers.why: A Montefiascone estate known for Est! Est!! Est!!! and for Montiano, a Merlot sold as IGT.

producers.name: Casale del Giglio
producers.why: An estate on the reclaimed Agro Pontino known for trials of international grapes such as Petit Verdot and for reviving Bellone.

exam: Lazio is the region of Rome: the Tyrrhenian Sea to the west, the Apennines to the east; maritime on the coast, continental inland.
Frascati: the Malvasia led white of the volcanic Castelli Romani, a DOC since 1966, with Frascati Superiore and Cannellino di Frascati DOCGs since 2011.
Know the three DOCGs as of 2026: Cesanese del Piglio (red, 2008), Frascati Superiore and Cannellino di Frascati (both white, 2011).
Cesanese is Lazio's native red, from Cesanese di Affile and Cesanese Comune; Piglio lies in the province of Frosinone.
Est! Est!! Est!!! di Montefiascone is the Procanico led white of Lake Bolsena, with its legend of the bishop's servant.
Volcanic soils run through the region: Bolsena, Vico, Bracciano and the Alban Hills.
Superiore means riper wine with a higher minimum alcohol; Riserva means longer ageing.
traps: Cannellino di Frascati is sweet; Frascati and Frascati Superiore are dry.
Cesanese del Piglio is the DOCG; Cesanese di Olevano Romano and Cesanese di Affile are DOCs.
Est! Est!! Est!!! is a white wine and a DOC, not a DOCG.
Malvasia del Lazio (Malvasia Puntinata) and Malvasia Bianca di Candia are two different vines; the first is the scented quality one.
The Orvieto DOC crosses into Lazio, but Orvieto is taught as Umbria's wine.
Montepulciano in a Roma red is the grape, not the Tuscan town of Vino Nobile.
Aleatico di Gradoli is Lazio's sweet red on Lake Bolsena; the Aleatico DOCG of Elba belongs to Tuscany.

cards.f: Lazio: climate and physical features
cards.b: Maritime on the Tyrrhenian coast, continental inland under the Apennines; volcanic hills and crater lakes from Bolsena to the Alban Hills.

questions.q: Which grape family leads the blend of Frascati?
questions.exp: Frascati is Malvasia led, Malvasia Bianca di Candia and Malvasia del Lazio together at least 70 per cent in the DOCGs; Trebbiano is a partner, Grechetto belongs to Orvieto and Vermentino to the coasts further north and to the islands.

questions.q: Under which name is the sweet, late harvest DOCG white of the Castelli Romani sold?
questions.exp: Cannellino di Frascati, raised to DOCG in 2011, is the sweet Frascati from late picked Malvasia led grapes, sometimes touched by noble rot.

questions.q: Which of these Lazio wines is the region's red DOCG?
questions.exp: Cesanese del Piglio, raised in 2008, is the red DOCG. Frascati Superiore and Cannellino di Frascati are the white DOCGs, and Est! Est!! Est!!! is a white DOC.

questions.q: In which year did Frascati become a DOC?
questions.exp: Frascati was approved as a DOC by a decree of March 1966, among Italy's first; its Superiore and Cannellino were raised to DOCG in 2011, the first DOCGs date from 1980 and 1992 is the year of the Goria law.

questions.q: Which town on Lake Bolsena gives its name to Est! Est!! Est!!!?
questions.exp: Est! Est!! Est!!! di Montefiascone, a DOC of 1966, is a Procanico led white from the hill town on the rim of the Bolsena crater.

questions.q: What kind of soil underlies the vineyards of Frascati?
questions.exp: The Castelli Romani sit on the rim of the old Alban volcano, so Frascati grows on light, porous volcanic ash and tuff rather than limestone, granite or schist.

questions.q: What is the minimum share of Montepulciano in Roma Rosso?
questions.exp: The Roma DOC, created in 2011, asks at least 50 per cent Montepulciano in its Rosso, with Cesanese and international grapes for the rest.

questions.q: Which red grape, a scented relation of Muscat, makes the sweet DOC wine of Gradoli on Lake Bolsena?
questions.exp: Aleatico di Gradoli is a sweet red of Aleatico, still or fortified as a liquoroso; Elba's Aleatico, in Tuscany, holds a DOCG of its own.

regions.name: Calabria and Basilicata
regions.summary: Two regions of the deep south, read together. Basilicata, the instep of Italy between Campania and Puglia, is mountain country whose one great wine is Aglianico del Vulture, grown on the slopes of an extinct volcano; its longer aged Superiore is the region's DOCG. Calabria, the toe, lies between the Tyrrhenian and Ionian seas, and its signature red is Cirò, from the pale but firm Gaglioppo on the Ionian coast; in 2025 Cirò Classico became Calabria's first DOCG. The south's Mediterranean heat is tempered by height and by the sea, and Greco di Bianco, a sweet wine from dried grapes, comes from near the tip of the toe.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean on the coasts: long, hot, dry summers and mild winters, with breezes off two seas. Inland the mountains change everything. On Monte Vulture in northern Basilicata the vineyards sit high enough for cold, snowy winters, a late spring and a wide swing between hot days and cool nights, so Aglianico ripens slowly and keeps its acidity. Calabria's coastal hills are hot and dry, the heat eased by sea air by day and by cool air falling from the mountains at night; the Sila and the Aspromonte above them take rain and snow in winter.
terroir.soils: Vulture's slopes are volcanic: layers of tuff, ash and lapilli over clay, free draining and rich in minerals, soft enough for cellars to be dug into them. Elsewhere in Basilicata the hills are clay, limestone and sand. Calabria's mountains are old crystalline rock, granite, gneiss and schist in the Sila, the Serre and the Aspromonte, while its coastal hills, Cirò among them, are clay, marl, sand and limestone.
terroir.topography: Basilicata is almost all mountain and hill, the southern Apennines, with two short coasts: a short stretch on the Tyrrhenian at Maratea and the plain of Metaponto on the Ionian. Monte Vulture rises alone in the north, near the borders with Campania and Puglia, and the vineyards climb its eastern and southern slopes. Calabria is a long, narrow peninsula of mountains that fall steeply to the sea on both sides, the Pollino in the north, the Sila plateau, the Serre and the Aspromonte at the toe, with little flat land; vines grow on the coastal hills and in the river valleys.
terroir.water: The Tyrrhenian Sea washes Calabria's west coast and Basilicata's short shore at Maratea; the Ionian Sea washes Calabria's east coast, where Cirò lies, and Basilicata's Metaponto plain. The Strait of Messina parts the toe from Sicily. Two lakes fill old craters on Vulture at Monticchio, and the Ofanto river passes to the north of the volcano.

grapes.name: Aglianico
grapes.styles: Basilicata's great red: late ripening, high in acid and firm in tannin, with black cherry, smoke and earth from Vulture's volcanic slopes; it needs years in cellar and bottle.

grapes.name: Gaglioppo
grapes.styles: Calabria's main red, the grape of Cirò: pale in colour but firm in tannin and often high in alcohol, with red cherry, dried herbs and spice; also rosato.

grapes.name: Magliocco
grapes.styles: A darker, softer Calabrian red, leading many wines of the Cosenza hills and the Tyrrhenian side and blended with Gaglioppo for colour and roundness.

grapes.name: Greco Bianco
grapes.styles: Calabria's name for the white of Cirò Bianco and of the sweet Greco di Bianco; a different vine from the Greco of Campania's Greco di Tufo.

grapes.name: Greco Nero
grapes.styles: A Calabrian red allowed beside Gaglioppo in Cirò, giving colour and fruit.

grapes.name: Mantonico
grapes.styles: Mantonico Bianco, an old Calabrian white made dry or as a sweet wine from dried grapes around Bianco.

grapes.name: Malvasia
grapes.styles: Malvasia Bianca di Basilicata and other Malvasias for whites under the Matera DOC and IGT Basilicata.

grapes.name: Zinfandel
grapes.styles: Grown as Primitivo in the province of Matera, for ripe, plummy reds under the Matera DOC.

wines.note: Deep and firm: black cherry, plum, smoke, tar and dried herbs, high acidity and strong tannin that need years to soften. Decant a young bottle and serve it with lamb, game or aged pecorino.
The DOC wine, released younger: dark fruit, earth and volcanic smoke with firm tannin; for grilled meats, sausages and pasta with a meat ragù.

Pale garnet but firm and warm: red cherry, orange peel, dried herbs and spice, with more tannin than its colour suggests. Serve it with grilled meats, spicy salami and the chilli of Calabrian cooking.
Gaglioppo made pink: dry, with red berries and herbs and enough grip for fish soups, grilled swordfish and summer vegetables.
Greco Bianco from the Ionian coast: fresh, with citrus, white flowers and almond, a glass for seafood and raw fish.
A golden to amber sweet wine from dried grapes: apricot, candied orange, honey and almond with a fresh finish. Pour it with almond pastries or blue cheese.

made.viticulture: Old vineyards in both regions are bush vines, alberello, which shade their own fruit in the heat; newer plantings are on wires, trained to spurred cordon or Guyot. On Vulture, Aglianico buds early and ripens late, so the harvest runs into late October and often November, and the free draining volcanic soil and the cool nights keep the grapes healthy and fresh through the long season; spring frost and autumn rain are the risks. Calabria's coastal vineyards face the opposite problem: heat and drought, met by bush training, picking early enough to hold acidity and, in newer vineyards, some irrigation. Much of both regions is still farmed in small plots by hand, and many old vineyards were abandoned in the twentieth century as people left the south. Growers and research collections in Calabria have rescued old local grapes such as Magliocco and Mantonico from neglect.
made.winemaking: Aglianico is made as a slow red: long maceration to extract and begin taming its tannin, then ageing in large casks of oak or chestnut by the traditional cellars and in barrique by the modern ones. The Superiore must spend at least twelve months in wood and twelve in bottle within its three years. The cellars of Barile and Rionero in Vulture are cut into the soft tuff, cool and damp all year. Cirò is traditionally fermented in cement or steel and aged in large old wood, giving a pale, savoury, tannic wine; the DOCG requires three years of ageing with at least six months in wood. Rosato is made from Gaglioppo with a short maceration. Greco di Bianco is made from grapes dried after picking until they shrivel and concentrate their sugar, then pressed and fermented into a sweet wine, a method shared with the sweet Mantonico.

law.classification: Each region now has one DOCG beside a short list of DOCs and IGTs. Basilicata's is Aglianico del Vulture Superiore, promoted in 2010 from the Aglianico del Vulture DOC of 1971: wholly Aglianico, at least 13.5 per cent alcohol and three years of ageing, five for the Riserva. The DOC continues for the younger wine, and Matera, Terre dell'Alta Val d'Agri and Grottino di Roccanova are the region's other DOCs, with IGT Basilicata covering the rest. Calabria had no DOCG until 2025, when the European Union registered Cirò Classico: a red of at least 90 per cent Gaglioppo, with Magliocco or Greco Nero, from the communes of Cirò and Cirò Marina, aged at least three years. The Cirò DOC of 1969 continues for reds and rosés of at least 80 per cent Gaglioppo and whites of at least 80 per cent Greco Bianco. Melissa, Savuto, Lamezia, Bivongi, Scavigna, Greco di Bianco and Terre di Cosenza are among Calabria's other DOCs, with IGT Calabria the broad tier.
